strengths: Addresses an important problem in end-to-end autonomous driving: uncertainty and non-determinism in planning. The motivation for probabilistic planning over deterministic regression is clear and well illustrated in Fig. 1.

Proposes a coherent vectorized architecture, VADv2, that takes streaming multi-view images, builds environmental token embeddings, and outputs a distribution over planning actions; the architecture is well presented and easy to follow.

Achieves strong closed-loop results on CARLA Town05 Long (Driving Score 85.1, Route Completion 98.4, Infraction Score 0.87) and Short benchmarks, outperforming several prior methods including some using LiDAR.

Ablation study attempts to isolate key components: distribution loss, conflict loss, and different scene tokens. It shows the distribution loss is crucial for open-loop planning accuracy (L2 and collision).
Provides qualitative visualizations of multi-modal planning in lane-changing, intersection, and car-following scenarios, supporting the claimed multi-modality.
The writing is generally clear and the related work is reasonably comprehensive, covering perception, motion prediction, planning, and LLM-based autonomous driving.

The planning vocabulary construction via furthest trajectory sampling is a sensible discretization strategy and allows soft supervision over candidate trajectories rather than only the ground-truth action.
The conflict loss incorporates safety priors via scene constraints, which is a reasonable way to regularize the predicted action distribution.
Only camera sensors are used at inference, and high-definition maps are not required in closed-loop evaluation, which is a practically desirable property.
The method demonstrates potential for flexible inference, e.g., top-K proposals with rule-based wrappers, which could be useful in real-world deployment.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited. Probabilistic planning over a discretized trajectory vocabulary is closely related to existing trajectory classification, anchor-trajectory prediction, mixture-of-experts, and language-model-inspired planning. The claim of being the 'first' to use probabilistic modeling for the continuous planning action space is overstated.

A central claim in the abstract, 'runs stably in a fully end-to-end manner, even without the rule-based wrapper,' is not quantitatively evaluated. The main CARLA benchmark results appear to use a rule-based wrapper, and no separate comparison without the wrapper is provided.

The ablation study lacks closed-loop metrics. Table 3 reports only open-loop L2 and collision rates, so it is not possible to verify whether probabilistic planning improves closed-loop driving performance compared to a deterministic baseline (e.g., ID 1) with the same architecture.

Inference is described inconsistently: the abstract says 'samples one action,' but the method section says it samples the highest-probability action (argmax) and uses a PID controller. True uncertainty sampling is not evaluated.

Evaluation is limited to CARLA Town05, with no real-world or additional benchmark results. Comparisons may be affected by differing wrappers, training budgets, and data, making the SOTA claim less conclusive.

The distribution loss is under-specified: it is unclear how the target data distribution p_data is constructed, how negative trajectory weights are set, and whether the KL divergence is well-defined for the soft target distribution.

Ablation differences are small for several components and no statistical significance or multiple random seeds are reported, so the necessity of every proposed loss and token type is weakly supported.
The conflict loss provides only marginal gains in the reported open-loop metrics, and its effect on safety-related closed-loop infractions is not analyzed.

Reproducibility is limited: no code release is mentioned, and key details such as loss coefficients, training schedule, model size, and compute requirements are missing. The 3-million-frame training set collection is not fully described.

The 'probabilistic field' and NeRF-inspired continuous modeling language is somewhat misleading because the final model is a discrete distribution over a fixed trajectory vocabulary, not a continuous probabilistic field over action space.

There is no direct comparison to a deterministic regression baseline using the same VADv2 architecture and training setup on closed-loop metrics, making it difficult to attribute gains to probabilistic planning rather than to architectural/token improvements.

Safety and ethical considerations for using a probabilistic planner in autonomous driving are not discussed. No safety guarantees, failure-case analysis, or discussion of potential collisions in real-world deployment is provided.

strengths: The paper reports strong empirical results: VADv2 achieves a Driving Score of 85.1 and Route Completion of 98.4 on CARLA Town05 Long using cameras only, which is a substantial improvement over prior SOTA such as DriveMLM (76.1/98.1) and DriveAdapter (71.9/97.3). These are meaningful margins on a well-known closed-loop benchmark.

The motivation for probabilistic planning is intuitive and clearly articulated: human driving is inherently stochastic, and deterministic regression to a single trajectory mode can be problematic when the feasible solution space is non-convex. Figure 1 illustrates this point effectively.

The use of a probabilistic field (inspired by NeRF-style continuous radiance fields) to map high-dimensional continuous trajectories to a distribution, combined with a discrete planning vocabulary, is technically reasonable and reasonably well described in the method section.
The ablation study (Table 3) attempts to quantify the contribution of the distribution loss, conflict loss, and different scene tokens, providing some evidence for the value of each component.
The paper is generally well-organized and the overall architecture (Figure 2) is clear.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental with respect to VAD [23]. The scene encoder (map/agent/traffic-element/image tokens, navigation and ego-state embeddings) is essentially carried over from VAD; the primary new elements are the planning-vocabulary discretization and the KL-based distribution loss. The paper does not clearly delineate which gains come from the new probabilistic formulation versus the reused architecture.

The central technical idea—discretizing a continuous action space into a codebook/vocabulary and learning a distribution over discrete modes—is closely related to long-standing anchor-based, VQ-codebook, and multi-modal (e.g., GMM/CVAE) trajectory prediction and planning methods, several of which are cited (e.g., MILE, GMM-based predictors). The claim of being 'the first work to use probabilistic modeling to fit the continuous planning action space' is therefore overstated and risks misrepresenting prior art.

At inference the model simply takes the highest-probability action ('we sample the action with the highest probability at each time step'), i.e., argmax. This undercuts the stated benefit of probabilistic planning at test time; the probabilistic formulation then functions mainly as a richer training signal. The paper does not empirically demonstrate any inference-time advantage of the distribution (e.g., via top-k proposals or uncertainty-based switching), only speculating about it in Section 3.4.

Reproducibility is limited. Key details are missing or vague: how exactly the furthest-trajectory sampling builds the vocabulary, the justification for N=4096, how the 'conflict check' and 'scene constraints' are instantiated, the sampling frequency/length of trajectories, and the weighting scheme for negative samples in the distribution and conflict losses.

The conflict loss relies on future ground-truth information (other agents' future motion, road boundaries) during training. This is a privileged-information setup that should be explicitly acknowledged and analyzed, but the paper presents it without discussing implications for deployment or for the fairness of comparisons.

The ablation (Table 3) is conducted only on open-loop L2 and collision metrics, whereas the main claims rest on closed-loop Driving Score. Open-loop metrics are known to correlate poorly with closed-loop performance in CARLA, so the ablation does not directly support the central claims. Closed-loop ablations are needed.

No run-to-run variance or multiple-seed results are reported. Closed-loop CARLA evaluation is notoriously high-variance and sensitive to hyperparameters and the rule-based wrapper; single-number comparisons (e.g., the 9.0-point gain over DriveMLM) are therefore not clearly statistically meaningful.

All reported driving results rely on a rule-based wrapper for conflict handling (Section 4.2). The abstract/introduction claim that VADv2 'runs stably in a fully end-to-end manner, even without the rule-based wrapper' is not backed by quantitative results in the tables, making it hard to attribute performance to the learned policy versus the wrapper.

The comparison set omits or only briefly discusses several directly relevant multi-modal planning baselines, and there is no analysis of failure modes (e.g., how often the closed-loop policy follows the wrong mode versus how often the wrapper corrects it).

Real-world generalization and out-of-distribution robustness remain unvalidated, which the authors acknowledge only briefly as future work, leaving the practical significance of the contribution uncertain.

strengths: Proposes a probabilistic planning framework for end-to-end driving that discretizes the action space into a planning vocabulary, tokenizes actions, and uses a transformer to predict an action distribution supervised by driving demonstrations and conflict losses.

Achieves strong closed-loop results: state-of-the-art on CARLA Town05 Long (DS 85.1, RC 98.4, IS 0.87) and leading or competitive results on Bench2Drive, NAVSIM, NAVSIMv2, and a 3DGS-based benchmark, using only camera sensors and no HD map at inference.

Comprehensive evaluation and ablation studies: key modules, planning manner (probabilistic vs. deterministic), traffic density, vocabulary size, training data amount, and vocabulary sampling strategies are analyzed.
Clear architecture and writing, with solid qualitative visualizations and code availability statement; addresses a practically important uncertainty issue in planning for autonomous driving.
The controlled deterministic-vs-probabilistic comparison and robustness analysis under different traffic densities provide useful evidence for the proposed planning paradigm.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is moderate: the core idea of discretizing trajectories/actions into a vocabulary and classifying/transformer-scoring them is close to existing token-based motion prediction and behavior cloning methods; the contribution is mainly an adaptation to end-to-end planning rather than a fundamentally new formulation.

The probabilistic formulation is mathematically inconsistent: p(a)=sigmoid(MLP(...)) is not normalized over the action vocabulary, yet KL divergence and cross-entropy are used as if it were a categorical distribution. This undermines the claimed probabilistic interpretation and could be fixed with a softmax over the vocabulary.

The main closed-loop benchmarks likely use a rule-based wrapper for fair comparison, while the abstract claims VADv2 runs stably in a fully end-to-end manner even without such a wrapper. No-wrapper results are not reported in the main paper, so this claim is not fully supported.
The real-world vehicle deployment is only stated to be in the supplementary material and is not quantitatively evaluated in the main text.

The conflict loss uses ground-truth future trajectories of other agents as privileged information during training, and its ablation gain appears small (e.g., ID2 vs. ID7), raising questions about its actual contribution and fairness.
Evaluation lacks error bars or multiple seeds for key results, and some claimed margins may not be statistically significant. Vocabulary generalization across datasets is only partially analyzed.
On the 3DGS-based benchmark, VADv2 does not achieve the best deviation ratio or average deviation distance, which weakens the broad safety claim compared with the collision-ratio improvement.

strengths: Addresses an important and well-motivated problem: the uncertainty and multimodality of human driving behavior, which are often overlooked by deterministic end-to-end planners.

Presents a clear and reasonably detailed architecture: scene tokenization (map, agent, traffic element, image tokens), planning vocabulary construction, and a planning transformer that predicts action probabilities.
Reports strong empirical results across several benchmarks (CARLA Town05, NAVSIM, Bench2Drive, 3DGS-based benchmark) and includes a substantial number of ablations on key design choices.

The ablation studies cover vocabulary size, training data scale, scene token variants, planning manner, multimodal outputs, and vocabulary sampling strategies, which helps understand the method’s components.
Attempts to validate beyond simulation with a 3DGS-based benchmark and a claim of real-world deployment, giving the work potential practical relevance.
The paper is generally well organized and provides implementation-level details such as token dimensions, trajectory horizon, and training setup.
weaknesses: The probabilistic modeling is technically unsound as written: p(a) is produced by a sigmoid independently for each action, with no softmax or normalization over the planning vocabulary. This does not define a valid probability distribution over mutually exclusive actions, and the KL-divergence/cross-entropy objective in Eq. 4–5 is mathematically unjustified in this form.

Because the distribution is not normalized, the central claim of ‘probabilistic planning’ is not convincingly supported. The model can trivially output high probabilities for many actions without being penalized by the distribution loss, and the learned scores are better described as discriminative rankings than as calibrated action probabilities.

At inference, the method selects the highest-probability action (argmax) rather than meaningfully sampling from the predicted distribution. This undermines the motivation around uncertainty modeling and non-deterministic planning; the reported closed-loop gains may come from a learned scorer plus rule-based post-processing rather than from probabilistic planning.

The paper contains contradictory claims about the rule-based wrapper. It states that VADv2 runs stably in a fully end-to-end manner without a rule-based wrapper, but the experimental section says a rule-based wrapper is adopted for fair comparison. It is unclear whether the main results use such a wrapper, which directly affects the strength of the end-to-end claim.

Evaluation fairness is questionable: some baseline numbers appear unexpectedly low (e.g., Transfuser DS 31.0 on Town05 Long), and the paper does not sufficiently clarify whether baselines were trained/evaluated under identical sensor, data, and post-processing conditions. Comparisons across different modalities and backbones are not fully controlled.

Novelty is limited. Discretizing trajectories/actions into a vocabulary and modeling them with token-based sequence models has already been explored in Trajeglish, MotionLM, and related work; VADv2 applies this idea to ego planning but does not provide a fundamentally new technical insight beyond the application setting.

Real-world claims are not substantiated in the main paper. The ‘real-world deployment’ results and the new 3DGS benchmark are largely relegated to the appendix, with no detailed safety analysis, failure cases, or quantitative real-vehicle results in the main text. The abstract’s strong real-world claims therefore outpace the evidence presented.

Most ablations rely on open-loop L2 and collision metrics, which are known to correlate imperfectly with closed-loop driving performance. The key closed-loop improvement is not broken down sufficiently to isolate the contribution of probabilistic planning from other factors such as the rule-based wrapper, PID controller, or additional scene-token supervision.

The conflict loss uses ground-truth future motion of other agents and road boundaries during training, which may introduce train-test mismatch and privileged information. The paper does not discuss how this affects deployment when such ground truth is unavailable.

Reproducibility is limited: the code URL is missing (‘Code is available at .’), the real-world dataset and 3DGS benchmark are not clearly released, and training uses 3M clips and 16 4090 GPUs, making independent reproduction difficult. Several implementation details remain vague.

Presentation issues remain: Algorithm 1 has possible off-by-one/unclear vocabulary construction logic, the ‘probabilistic field’ terminology is not formally defined, and some claims (e.g., leading all benchmarks) are overstated when VADv2 is not best on all reported metrics (e.g., efficiency/comfort on Bench2Drive, some NAVSIM metrics).

strengths: The paper addresses an important and well-motivated problem: modeling uncertainty and multimodality in end-to-end driving planning, contrasting with deterministic regression policies.

It introduces a clear probabilistic planning formulation that discretizes the action space into a planning vocabulary, learns a scene-conditioned distribution over complete trajectories, and uses cross-entropy/conflict losses; the design is intuitive and integrates well with tokenized scene representations.

Evaluation is extensive and convincing: strong state-of-the-art results on CARLA Town05 Long/Short, Bench2Drive, NAVSIM, NAVSIMv2, and a 3DGS-based benchmark, often with camera-only inputs compared to camera+LiDAR baselines.

The ablation studies are thorough, covering design choices (distribution/conflict loss, scene tokens), vocabulary size, training data scale, multimodal outputs, probabilistic vs. deterministic planning, and vocabulary sampling strategies.
The method is presented with sufficient architectural and implementation details, and the authors state code will be available, supporting reproducibility.

The paper demonstrates practical significance with large-scale training data, real-world-inspired 3DGS evaluation, and deployment-oriented discussion, making it relevant to autonomous driving and robust planning.
weaknesses: The 'probabilistic field' framing overstates the method: in practice VADv2 is a categorical classifier over a fixed vocabulary of 4096 complete trajectories rather than a continuous density over the full action space. Inference is restricted to the vocabulary, and no quantitative analysis of coverage for out-of-vocabulary or long-tail maneuvers is provided.

The claim of fully end-to-end and real-world deployment is not fully substantiated in the main paper: closed-loop benchmark results use a rule-based wrapper for fair comparison, and real-world vehicle results are deferred to supplementary material without quantitative closed-loop evidence.

The evaluation lacks variance/statistical significance and does not compare against stronger multimodal or probabilistic planning baselines (e.g., mixture density networks, diffusion/flow-based planners) in all key benchmarks; the deterministic baseline is a single MLP regressor rather than a strong multimodal deterministic alternative.

The conflict loss relies on ground-truth future motion and road boundaries during training, and the inference-time 'Conflict Check' shown in Figure 2 is not clearly specified algorithmically; this makes the safety-claim mechanism difficult to reproduce or assess.
Some benchmark numbers and settings are potentially inconsistent or under-explained, and the self-constructed 3DGS benchmark lacks full detail for independent reproduction.

The training target uses hard best-matched trajectory labels for cross-entropy, with no ablation on soft labels or assignment strategies; this may limit probabilistic calibration and multimodal coverage in ambiguous scenarios.
